title: Show HN: Lockward – a lockfile for skills and MCP servers your AI agent loads
story_key: story|title:lockward a lockfile for skills and mcp servers your ai agent loads
content_excerpt: Lockward pins every skill, MCP server, hook and rules file your AI coding agents load, then blocks anything that changes without approval. It works offline across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Gemini CLI, and outputs SARIF and CycloneDX AI-BOMs. Think of it as a lockfile plus a CI policy gate for agent supply chains. Lockward pins every skill, MCP server, hook, rules file and security-relevant setting used by Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Windsurf and GitHub Copilot, then fails locally or in CI when anything changes without approval. It runs offline, needs no account, and has no LLM in the loop. Scanners tell you what looks bad today. Lockward tells you what changed since you approved it, and blocks it. AI agents load third-party skills, MCP servers, hooks and instruction files that run with your shell, files and credentials. In 2026 that layer became an actively attacked supply chain: over a thousand malicious skills in one marketplace, MCP packages that turned malicious after 15 clean versions, repositories whose config auto-executes when opened, and public demonstrations that every major skill scanner can be bypassed. The common recommendation is to pin what you trust, review every change and keep an inventory. Lockward makes that a single CI step. Background and sources: docs/RESEARCH.md . Approve only what you reviewed: lockward approve <id> updates that entry and nothing else. The action downloads the release, verifies its Sigstore signature and checksum before running it, writes a job summary, and uploads SARIF so each drifted item and policy finding shows up in code scanning. It is listed on the GitHub Marketplace as Lockward Verify (source: Breaktroughf1/lockward-action ). verify and scan-repo can also attach findings from external scanners such as SkillSpector, Cisco skill-scanner or Snyk with --scanner-sarif (informational; they never change the exit code). Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 drift, 2 policy violation, 3 usage or configuration error, 4 internal error. Full reference: docs/USAGE.md . What gets pinned. Every file in a skill, including dotfiles, binaries and archives, hashed in full however large it is; MCP server definitions (command, arguments, package and version, URL, and environment and header names , never values); hooks and the scripts they call; rules and instruction files at any depth; and the settings that grant permissions, such as auto-approval lists. Paths were checked against each agent's documentation on 2026-11-23: do

summary_1line: Lockward is an open-source tool that pins AI coding agents' skills, MCP servers, hooks and rules files, then fails local or CI runs when pinned items change without approval.

title: Chainguard's Dan Lorenc: Inside the PHP2Shell Disclosure
summary:
AI models are finding years of hidden bugs in open source, and Chainguard's Dan Lorenc says the only way out is software automation: point your agents at your upgrades before attackers point theirs at your code.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:

Dan explains why Chainguard shipped its PHP2Shell fix once attacks appeared in the wild, ahead of the official patch, why most exploitable bugs never get a CVE, and why the Linux kernel now files one for every bug fix. Then stay for Dan's full DevCon talk, What Breaks First on the Way to Machine Speed: A Macro and Micro View.

– Black October: PHP2Shell, Brotli, GitLab and the Glasswing disclosure wave

title: What broke in 27 days of running a team of AI agents on real work
story_key: story|title:what broke in 27 days of running a team of ai agents on real work
content_excerpt: I made a 95-second film of an ordinary day with my agents ( ethanflow.com/how-i-work ). Every scene in it was re-enacted on the live system, with names and conversations changed, and the film says so on screen. A film shows the parts that work. This post is about the parts that broke, which is where most of my time goes. The setup: since October 31, a coordinator session has run on my Mac every day, from morning into the evening. It is a Claude Code session with a written manual. It splits requests into briefs, hands them to worker sessions or short-lived sub-agents, checks what comes back, and reports to me in a group chat on my phone. The work is ordinary: reading and drafting email, shipping updates to my apps, keeping a few servers alive, research, and repairing its own tooling. There is one hard wall, payments. It fills everything in up to checkout and stops. The model is rented. Everything around it I built, and that is the part that breaks. A busy day of chat, reports and tool output fills the window by mid-afternoon. A hook warns at 70% and again at 85%. The coordinator then writes a handoff file (what’s pending, which workers are running, whether the listener is armed), opens a fresh session and tells it to read the file. In 27 days there have been 35 coordinator sessions. The rule that makes this survivable: state lives on disk, not in the conversation. Every wake-up is read disk, act, write back. What still broke: The coordinator never polls in a loop of its own. A small client I call the listener holds a long-poll against the chat server and exits when something arrives. The exit ends a background job, and that wakes the session. The most useful bug I’ve had came from someone else’s agent. The chat service my coordinator reports through is AndCo, which I built so that people and their own AIs can share groups, and other users’ agents run the same listener script. On November 2 we found that one user’s agent had been deaf for 19 days. As far as we could tell it ran our client; either its credentials had been rotated and the server answered 403, or a proxy connection had hung. The client handled 401 and nothing else. Any other failure meant: wait 15 seconds, try again, write nothing, never exit. Its owner had been calling it in a group for two days before anyone noticed. The fix: log every non-401 failure to stderr (the first at once, then at most one line every five minutes), and after ten minutes of continuous failure, exit with code 2. Exiting

title: Show HN: AI agents explore your mobile app, then their paths replay as tests
story_key: story|title:ai agents explore your mobile app then their paths replay as tests
content_excerpt: 20 AI testers on 20 different phones, in parallel, on GitHub's free runners: Claude Code agents on iOS Simulators and Android emulators that find broken flows, translation, layout and accessibility bugs The phones are real screen recordings of the LocalSend run; the map is the dashboard on the demo app . Video with sound (MP4) · The 20 phones, full recording · The run, device by device No test scripts to write. Each tester is a Claude Code agent with its own iOS Simulator or Android emulator on GitHub Actions. It plays a persona (iPhone SE in Swedish at the largest text size, Pixel 7 at 200%, iPad in German, Arabic right to left...), uses your app like a new user (or runs through the feature you point it at) and writes a bug report with screenshots. Flutter, React Native, Expo, native Kotlin and Swift, Kotlin Multiplatform, Capacitor and .NET MAUI. GitHub's runners are free for public repos. You only pay for the model, with your Claude subscription or API key: about $0.15 to $0.55 per phone in these runs . Or let Claude set it up for you: /plugin marketplace add pierridotite/mobile-agent-testers , then /plugin install mobile-agent-testers@mobile-agent-testers . Every input (builds, briefs, bug reports, cheaper models, build arguments, video) and the supported frameworks: docs/configuration.md . The demo app has 11 deliberate bugs . In one run , the 4 demo testers found 9 of them (2 to 7 minutes per agent, about 21 minutes for the whole run, builds included), plus real issues nobody planted (a button under the Android nav bar, no data kept after a relaunch). Model usage: $0.87 for the 4. Each persona explores your app like a new user and reports what gets in the way, with numbered screenshots. A run can also follow one feature end to end, reproduce a bug report, write an improvement report, compare two versions or test a website on phones. One use per run, set with the inputs above. Any Anthropic-compatible model works, from Claude Haiku to OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, MiniMax or Qwen; findings are only as good as the model's reading of screenshots ( docs/cheaper-models.md ). Maestro or Appium run the tests you write; these agents look for what nobody thought to test ( how it compares ). Every screen the testers reached, with the path of each one in its own color and a heat map of where they tapped. title: Why I'm Bullish on MCP for 2027
summary: Early MCP deserved its backlash. Code Mode, typed outputSchema, native multimodality, Agent Skills inside MCP, always-on MCP Events, and MCP Apps are turning it into the integration layer for agent harnesses in 2027.
story_key: story|title:why i m bullish on mcp for 2027
content_excerpt: MCP went through the full hype cycle in the last 18 months. Early excitement turned into backlash and confusion fast, with context bloat as the main complaint. When Skills arrived, most developers moved to CLIs and progressive disclosure instead. I never believed in that, and that sentiment is now changing. At Linear and Notion , agents now create roughly half of all issues (~2.4M/week) and pages, with Notion reporting 60x MCP traffic growth. At Atlassian , MCP handles over 5M tool calls per workday, and 44% of those users sit outside software teams where CLIs were never an option. At Neon , agent usage over MCP grows 14% week over week, and even Apple now ships local MCP servers for Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. The protocol is healthy and actively improving. The 2026-07-28 spec dropped stateful sessions and added official extensions, and clients are getting smarter about how they use them. Real tasks almost always take more than 1 tool call, e.g. you list open issues, grab details, check errors, and write a summary. With plain tool calling, every step needs another model turn and dumps information into the context. Joining data across 2 MCP servers uses the model's context as memory for intermediate payloads. Code Mode is changing how agents call MCP servers. Instead of putting 50 tool schemas into the prompt and calling 1 tool per turn, the harness gives the model a sandbox and exposes MCP tools as callable functions. It's already becoming the default in OpenCode 2.0, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Pi, and Factory Droid. Code Mode works best when the model knows what a tool returns before writing code. When an MCP server declares outputSchema alongside inputSchema , the client can generate typed stubs upfront and pass back structuredContent directly. The model chains multiple calls in 1 script, filters and joins in memory where compute is cheap, and returns only what matters. Compared to CLIs, MCP servers are natively multimodal. A tool call can return typed structuredContent for code alongside separate image, audio, or embedded resource blocks. Auth is also cleaner. CLIs and raw curl force you to store API keys on disk or in environment variables with broad permissions. An MCP client handles per-user OAuth 2.1 login flows and scoped tool permissions outside the sandbox, so connecting a remote SaaS product works without handing raw credentials to the agent. The debate of Skills plus a CLI versus MCP might come to an end as well. So far teams shipped CLIs or

title: RoboEvo$^2$: Recursive Robot Self-Improvement via Harness-Policy Co-Evolution
summary: Robots should adapt to unfamiliar environments and acquire new skills through interaction, then execute those skills efficiently with practice. Vision-language-action policies provide efficient control, but often need additional human demonstrations to handle unfamiliar settings; reasoning agents can discover solutions using broad prior knowledge and robot-control APIs, but repeated deliberation and repair are costly. Inspired by human learning through reasoning and practice, we propose RoboEvo$^2$, a framework for recursive harness-policy co-evolution. In Policy-to-Harness (P2H) evolution, policy failures guide a coding agent to search complementary Code, Code+ICL, and Code+Policy routes, consolidating verified solutions into reusable skills, routing strategies, and experience memory. In Harness-to-Policy (H2P) evolution, verified trajectories provide supervised training, while Counterfactual Preference Distillation (CPD) teaches the policy to favor successful corrections over failures from the same starting state. The improved policy provides stronger motor skills for subsequent search, while its remaining failures redirect harness evolution, closing the reciprocal loop. Through recursive co-evolution without additional human demonstrations, RoboEvo$^2$ improves standalone success from 11.0% to 84.1% and hybrid success from 30.4% to 90.5% on LIBERO-PRO, with similar gains and reduced agentic costs on RoboTwin C2R. Further experiments demonstrate autonomous task acquisition, cross-embodiment harness transfer, and 95.0% hybrid success on the Unitree G1-D. Our models and code will be publicly released.

title: Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference
story_key: model:nemotron|ver:3.5|title:building on nemotron 3 5 parse open data fine tuning and faster inference
content_excerpt: We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading

title: Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks
summary: The emerging field of weight space learning has demonstrated the potential to enable metanetworks, i.e. models that process neural network (NN) data, to support several steps of the machine learning lifecycle, from model optimisation to evaluation and adaptation. However, this potential has yet to materialise beyond small-scale MLPs or CNNs: most current models, including message-passing based graph metanetworks (GMNs), operate exclusively at the finest level of granularity, processing every neuron and weight of the input model. Their cost therefore scales with the number of parameters. Yet NNs are inherently organised hierarchically, with neurons forming layers and layers forming blocks and modules. Additionally, several of their properties, such as Lipschitz upper bounds and generalisation measures, are compositions of layer- and block-level quantities. To incorporate this inductive bias, we introduce Hierarchical Graph Metanetworks (H-GMNs), which leverage the input architecture's hierarchy to coarsen and refine the graph using permutation-symmetry-preserving pooling and un-pooling layers. Further, we extend H-GMNs to Transformers by introducing a graph construction that preserves permutation symmetries and enables multi-level pooling. Our evaluation includes new ResNet-18, ViT and varying ViT model zoos of up to 86M parameters, on tasks spanning model evaluation (an analytic Lipschitz bound proxy, generalisation and robustness prediction), testing (backdoor detection) and editing (pruning). Experimental results show that, compared to non-equivariant alternatives and flat GMNs, H-GMNs are markedly more sample-efficient, and their cost remains nearly constant as metanetwork depth grows, allowing deeper and more expressive processing where flat GMNs run out of memory, without compromising accuracy, which in certain cases considerably improves.

title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

title: HOG-WAM: Improving Visual Robustness through Future Gradient Prediction
summary: World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions, yet visual corruption can disrupt the resulting policies. We introduce HOG-WAM, which adds future Histograms of Oriented Gradients (HOG) as structural supervision derived directly from demonstration images. An auxiliary HOG diffusion transformer (DiT) module reads RGB features through asymmetric attention, allowing its objective to shape the visual representation used for control. The module is used only during training and removed at inference, preserving FastWAM's RGB-to-action architecture. We evaluate four controlled observation corruptions through a visual-corruption extension of RoboTwin, termed RoboTwin-Plus; HOG-WAM achieves the highest success among the compared policies under all four. Mixed-noise success increases from 78.86% to 82.86% relative to FastWAM, with comparable performance on clean scenes. On LIBERO Plus, overall success increases from 74.49% to 75.26%, with the largest gain under sensor noise, from 74.14% to 78.89%. Across four Franka tasks, average success increases from 40% to 59% under clean observations and from 17% to 24% under noisy observations. A representation ablation favors combining RGB observations with auxiliary HOG prediction over replacing RGB with HOG. These findings support future-gradient prediction as complementary supervision for visually robust control, with larger absolute gains on physical tasks than in simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/HOG-WAM.

title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
summary: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.

title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba55afd0>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba558e90>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba559510>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba55a450>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba55a510>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba55b510>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE TABLE customer_feedback ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, comment TEXT ); INSERT INTO customer_feedback (customer_name, comment) VALUES ('Alice', 'I was charged twice on my credit card! Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9aba55b7d0>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

title: claude-code v2.1.329
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a trust dialog warning that says where a folder's hooks are declared
  • Added a warning in the conversation, in Claude Desktop and other non-interactive hosts, when hooks in managed settings fail to load
  • Added this session's scheduled tasks, /loop wakeups, the goal and this conversation's forks to /tasks; x stops one after asking
  • Added a "Server message" row to a server's page in /mcp that shows the JSON-RPC error message of a remote HTTP MCP server that refuses the connection
  • Added a "Marketplace auto-update" row to /status that names managed marketplaces that get no automatic updates, and why
  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while OpenTelemetry events and metrics are enabled; each tool call the code makes sends its events; tracing still keeps it off
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json sometimes being reset to defaults when a network stall or file lock made it unreadable and cleared during a save
  • Fixed repeated sign-outs on macOS when Claude Code could read the Keychain but not save to it. That session now stops at expiry and says why, and other sessions stay signed in
  • Fixed /terminal-setup corrupting VS Code settings or keybindings files around block comments, and reporting success while losing the Shift+Enter binding where keybindings.json has an unclosed string
  • Fixed files accepted through the IDE diff being saved without their last newline, and losing their byte order mark (BOM) when an edit was accepted by saving the diff in VS Code
  • Fixed picking a cloud session in /teleport replacing your open conversation: the pick now starts a new session, as /clear does, and /resume brings the old one back
  • Fixed /usage-credits asking Pro and Max users to log in again after opening the browser, and the link disappearing after 8 seconds if the browser doesn't open and a task stops for usage credits
  • Fixed /usage saying usage credits are off when they had run out or reached the monthly limit, and /model not telling Pro and Max users when that limit blocks a model that runs on usage credits
  • Fixed the spend limit menu showing your spend as your monthly limit and wrapping its rows under the pointer in narrow windows
  • Fixed a status line script that prints without end freezing the prompt and using gigabytes of memory
  • Fixed an empty, frozen screen after approving managed settings while the --resume picker, the trust dialog or another set-up screen was waiting
  • Fixed choosing Default in /model replacing your saved model with your organization's default when the Default row already showed your saved model
  • Fixed an MCP server being signed in again after you cleared its authentication while a token refresh was running
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stalled after a slow reconnect: Claude Code now reconnects most HTTP MCP servers by itself when one is left on an older protocol version
  • Fixed PDFs, images and .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files that MCP servers or websites send as application/octet-stream being saved as .bin, which kept Claude from reading the PDFs and images
  • Fixed /code-review <pr number> sometimes reviewing the checked-out branch instead of the pull request without saying so: it now reads the pull request with gh pr diff, or says when it can't
  • Fixed /code-review stopping at a permission prompt, on most models, to look for a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that doesn't exist
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --push-outcome-on-release sometimes deleting a session's branch on the git host
  • Fixed Code Mode hiding a script's finished edits and the stopped command after Esc, and losing them on exit
  • Fixed a runaway loop in Code Mode filling the machine's memory; it is now stopped at a limit
  • Fixed a background agent running on when it was stopped while it was being resumed
  • Fixed background shell commands using memory for the earlier conversation until they exit
  • Fixed Remote Control using memory for the earlier conversation after a compaction or /clear in sessions run by Claude Desktop, IDEs or the SDK
  • Fixed Stop not ending a request in Claude Desktop sessions on Bedrock while it waits on a hung AWS credential_process or sign-in call
  • Fixed Claude sometimes failing to send you a file on its first try on Opus 4.8 and Opus 5
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a connected MCP server's tools could not be loaded, and taking it for a server with no tools, in sessions with tool search
  • Fixed claude mcp login and /mcp saying a service doesn't accept sign-ins from Claude Code when the service's client registration had been retired (HTTP 410 Gone)
  • Fixed another case of claude.ai-synced plugin hooks failing with "Plugin directory does not exist" while a session was still running on macOS
  • Fixed auto mode asking for manual approval to rm a symlink that points outside the working directory or at itself
  • Fixed /sandbox on Linux listing allowUnixSockets entries as allowed: they don't open those sockets there, and /sandbox now says so
  • Fixed pressing Esc twice to clear a mistyped code ending the sign-in in /install-github-app
  • Remote Control: Fixed sessions going back to their first effort level after a restart while the app still showed the level you picked (not yet for sessions that start in Ultracode)
  • Fixed a removed plugin's MCP server staying connected in headless sessions after reload_plugins or when the account's plugin list drops it
  • Fixed the Claude Docs connector's tools going missing when a plugin or MCP server at the same address failed to connect, and its error wrongly suggesting /login
  • Fixed a new skills, commands or agents folder being missed when --add-dir names the working directory or Claude Code starts in the home folder
  • Fixed sessions started from a pre-warmed process ignoring the autoCompactWindow setting in the project's .claude/settings.json
  • Fixed CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE staying in effect in a running session after it is removed from settings.json
  • Fixed the Agent tool's effort parameter being ignored for named teammates in agent teams
  • Fixed /auto-mode-setup ignoring recent auto mode denials when it scans a project for rules to suggest; it may now offer allow rules from them, and you review each before it's saved
  • Fixed a false "Couldn't save this change" warning after adding a permission rule or directory in a subfolder or worktree whose own .claude/settings.local.json is unreadable or malformed
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude to run a network proxy check after a failed request, which auto mode then blocked
  • Fixed headless rewind and fork going ahead while a message sent right after a model change still waited on it
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a background task was stopped while a cloud session was restarting
  • Fixed /team-onboarding reporting a guide as shared on Team and Enterprise plans when the server refused the upload
  • Fixed panels and questions being cut off at the prompt in fullscreen, /help, history search and the background tasks list losing rows or titles in short windows, and tables wrapping in dialogs
  • Fixed resumed sessions showing "Rejected" or "Declined" for edits, questions and plans that were cut off when the session ended
  • Fixed /passes showing the wrong number of passes after a server error, and offering usage credits for sharing when no guest passes are left
  • Fixed claude --help output being cut short when piped to another program
  • Fixed /terminal-setup turning on "Use Option as Meta key" in Terminal.app on macOS 27, and tips there suggesting Option+Enter instead of Shift+Enter
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed setup failing on Git LFS repositories cloned through Anthropic-managed git; sessions now start on pointer files, and git lfs pull fetches the content
  • Fixed sessions on self-hosted environments not starting from a git remote with an SSH host alias, GitHub SSH certificates or a GHE.com SSH user; an unresolved alias's error gives two git commands
  • Fixed remote MCP servers in self-hosted runner sessions staying without tools, or (over https) disconnected, after a timeout or network error
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as having stopped responding while Claude Code was still starting
  • Fixed Code Mode keeping in memory every large text file that code read, and memory growing each time a background subagent was woken
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script at its ten-minute limit while an MCP form, an MCP link prompt or a prompt that always asks was waiting for an answer
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts receiving a "moved to the background" message as data from most MCP calls over two minutes: the script now waits up to ten minutes, then gets an error
  • Fixed mods that list only some tools silently turning Code Mode off; such a mod no longer keeps it off, so use managed settings for that
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn when the tool was called from a script that Claude waits for
  • Fixed a Code Mode script's let x; keeping the value that an earlier script gave x
  • Fixed a Code Mode script's call with no argument failing with a missing-parameter error on tools that need none
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts losing access to tools through tools in sessions with more than 4,096 tools
  • Fixed the /code-review findings card often showing "high" for a review that ran at medium, on most models
  • Fixed key hints in permission prompts, questions, /model and /rewind ignoring keybindings.json
  • Fixed auto-scroll, the PR status badge, the auto-compact warning and the ultracode tag not following the /config switches that control them in a running session
  • Fixed a custom cancel key not working in /add-dir, /tui feedback and the save-workflow form
  • Fixed arrow keys in the save-workflow form moving the selection in the workflow view behind it
  • Fixed /config saying nothing, or "dismissed", after changing many settings
  • Fixed Read and @-mentions showing one line too many for files that end in a newline
  • Fixed /status not naming the model that opusplan and haiku use in plan mode
  • Fixed claude doctor advising a Keychain unlock inside a macOS sandbox, where unlocking can't help
  • Fixed the "Jump to bottom" pill staying hidden after copying text and scrolling away, the row under it going blank when its label changed, and quick PageUp presses scrolling too far in fullscreen
  • Fixed a screen update sometimes being skipped when memory is low
  • Fixed long code blocks losing a blank line and repeating another in scrollback
  • Fixed prompt suggestions sometimes showing placeholder text such as _(no suggestion)_
  • Fixed the line about earlier messages on resume blaming a damaged file when the file was intact
  • Fixed characters disappearing from the prompt when its text held a color code that sets several styles and a keyword or command was highlighted
  • Fixed /rename and UserPromptSubmit hook titles in claude remote-control sessions not showing on claude.ai and mobile
  • Fixed the Remote Control diff listing a file twice when the branch renamed it and it was then edited
  • Improved the automatic clean-up of old sessions on computers with managed settings
  • Improved /tui and other in-place restarts to wait briefly for a login refresh, so they are less likely to sign you out
  • Improved memory use in long sessions that edit many files, and in long Claude Desktop sessions on macOS and Linux with many large MCP tool results
  • Windows: Improved start-up and the first search on PCs where Claude Code's search program starts slowly
  • Improved auto mode's handling of a short reply such as "yes" to Claude's question when telemetry is off, behind a gateway to the Anthropic API, or on Microsoft Foundry
  • Improved memory use of idle Claude Desktop and SDK sessions after a long turn, and after --resume or --continue of a session that holds screenshots or large tool results
  • Improved how fast a Claude Desktop Code session with Remote Control on is ready for the next message after an answer
  • Improved cloud sessions to retry plugins that failed to download at startup
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Improved Code Mode: after starting a subagent, Claude now gets the same guidance on waiting as outside Code Mode
  • Updated computer use on macOS to newer safety rules, so some actions are refused and some apps have less access
  • Changed saved scheduled tasks: in new signed-in sessions, most saved by earlier versions need scheduling again, though --resume of their own session still runs them
  • Changed /code-review with no target on most models to review the whole branch against the default branch, and fixed it losing the diff on multi-commit branches
  • Changed auto mode to run git status less often so most requests wait less in large repositories; a git command that discards changes may be blocked until the working tree is checked
  • Changed /code-review <pr number> --fix, and /code-review given a pull request URL, to stop without reviewing when gh pr diff is refused or fails
  • Changed 'Exit and stop tasks' to end this session's scheduled tasks so they don't run again on resume, unless you exit while Claude is responding
  • Changed some teammate panes to start through /bin/sh, so they may not read shell start-up files
  • Changed computer use on macOS to give up on an app launch that has not finished after 30 seconds
  • Gateway: Changed the start-up warning shown while access_control.allow_cidrs is empty to a notice at every start, boxed in text logs: never expose the gateway to the public internet
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a second host name's clone of the same owner/name to go under _repos/clones/<host>/ in the base folder; no clone moves
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed repositories with unusual characters in their address path to clone anew in a new folder; rules and volumes naming the old one stop applying, and the old clone stays put
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed --repository-folder to take most folders in the base folder at --capacity 1 (above 1, one there stops start-up); another repository's session overlapping one is refused
  • Changed Code Mode so a PreToolUse hook that errors no longer refuses a script's tool call, as outside Code Mode; set "onFailure": "block" on a command, HTTP or MCP tool hook that must refuse
  • Changed Code Mode to refuse a script's read of a line range over 256 MiB, which could use gigabytes of memory, and fixed reads of very long lines timing out
  • Changed Code Mode to also start when telemetry, nonessential traffic or feature flags are turned off; an administrator can keep it off in managed settings
  • Changed Code Mode to run a script that declares its own log, preview or sleep, which it used to refuse
  • Changed macOS login renewal to test the Keychain with a Claude Code-write-check item
  • Changed the /tasks header and the footer's background count to one number covering shells, monitors, MCP calls, agents, workflows and scheduled tasks
  • Changed Stop and SubagentStop hooks to list a Monitor's script as monitor, not shell, in background_tasks
  • Removed 2.1.326's automatic retry at the limit named in a max_tokens error; behind a gateway whose model takes fewer output tokens, set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS to that limit
  • [VSCode] Added a line above the message box after you decline the trust prompt, with Review trust to bring the prompt back without reloading the window
  • [VSCode] Fixed being signed out of Claude Code in every window and terminal when the sign-in server took 10 to 30 seconds to answer the extension's token refresh
  • [VSCode] Fixed keys pressed while an input method (IME) is composing moving focus on or declining a permission prompt, running menu rows and closing dialogs (#106358)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for Bash, Edit, Write and other built-in tools not showing why a safety check asks
  • [VSCode] Fixed a half-written plan comment being lost or moved to another passage, and an input method's Enter sending the comment, ending a session rename or picking an @-mentioned file
  • [VSCode] Fixed the limit banner not saying when usage credits are in use, and the session survey covering that banner and the usage credits card
  • [VSCode] Fixed screen readers not announcing a permission request that arrived while the Account & Usage dialog was open until that dialog was closed
  • [VSCode] Fixed a proposed-edit diff tab staying open, with an Accept button that did nothing, after its terminal Claude Code session disconnected
  • [VSCode] Fixed short tool inputs and outputs cut off at the panel's edge with no way to read the rest (they now open in an editor tab), and dragging to select text also opening one
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Up key putting an earlier message over text that an input method (IME) is composing in the message box (#101294)
  • [VSCode] Fixed dropping an Explorer folder onto the chat inserting nothing on VS Code 1.103 to 1.139 or in a floating chat window, and the drop highlight vanishing with a false "Hold Shift" hint
  • [VSCode] Fixed a permission prompt moving keyboard focus away from the details you were scrolling as its buttons switched on
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening in another editor group when claudeCode.lockEditorGroups is off (#108884)
  • [VSCode] Fixed ranges written with a single tilde (3~5 … 7~10) losing their tildes and showing struck-through text between them; only ~~text~~ is struck through now
  • [VSCode] Fixed dictation errors wrapping into a narrow column, the spinner turning while a question card waits, and a NUL symbol after each letter in the output of a failed UTF-16 command
  • [VSCode] Changed Down to stop at the last item of a permission prompt instead of wrapping to Yes
  • [VSCode] Changed command output to show hidden characters and control sequences other than plain colors as symbols, so Persian, Khmer, Lao, Sinhala and Malayalam text can look broken or out of order
